## Using gtsummary for Professional Tables

gtsummary creates publication-ready tables from R data.

### Basic Summary Table

```{r}
library(gtsummary)

data <- gtsummary::trial
# Summary table
data %>% 
  tbl_summary(by = trt) %>% 
  add_p()
```

### Regression Tables

```{r}
# Logistic regression example
data$outcome <- rbinom(200, 1, 0.5)

model_log <- glm(outcome ~ age + trt, data = data, family = binomial)

tbl_regression(model_log, exponentiate = TRUE)
```

### Customizing Tables

```{r}
data %>% 
  tbl_summary(
    by = trt,
    statistic = list(
      all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
      all_categorical() ~ "{n} ({p}%)"
    )
  ) %>% 
  add_p(test = all_continuous() ~ "t.test") %>%   # mean (SD) shown, so compare means
  modify_header(label = "**Variable**") %>% 
  bold_labels()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Match the test to the summary
`add_p()` compares numbers with a **rank-based** test by default (Wilcoxon, Kruskal–Wallis). If the table shows **mean (SD)**,
set the test to `"t.test"` (or `"oneway.test"` for 3 or more groups), as above; otherwise the table shows means but tests ranks.
:::

### Table 1 for a study (NCD survey)

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
ncd <- read_csv(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv")[file.exists(c("../data/ncd_survey.csv", "data/ncd_survey.csv"))][1], show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(sex = factor(sex), htn = factor(htn, 0:1, c("No", "Yes")))

ncd |>
  select(age, sex, residence, bmi, sbp, tobacco, htn) |>
  tbl_summary(by = htn,
              label = list(age ~ "Age (years)", bmi ~ "BMI (kg/m²)", sbp ~ "Systolic BP (mmHg)"),
              statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{median} ({p25}, {p75})", all_categorical() ~ "{n} ({p}%)"),
              digits = all_continuous() ~ 1,
              missing_text = "Missing") |>
  add_overall() |>
  add_p() |>
  bold_labels()
```

-   **`by =`** splits the columns by group; **`add_overall()`** adds a total column.
-   **`statistic =`** chooses the summary: `"{mean} ({sd})"` for roughly symmetric variables, `"{median} ({p25}, {p75})"` for skewed ones.
-   **`missing_text`** shows how many values are missing for each variable; **do not hide them**.
-   **`add_p()`** picks a test for each variable (Wilcoxon, t-test, chi-square, Fisher) and **footnotes which one**.

### Reading Table 1

-   **Table 1 describes the sample**; it is not where the findings go (models and effects belong in later tables).
-   Give **n (%)** for categories and **mean (SD)** or **median (IQR)** for numbers; say which in the footnote.
-   In a **randomised trial**, do **not** report p-values for baseline differences: any difference is by chance. Use standardised differences if you need a check.
-   In an **observational** study, p-values for exposure groups are descriptive; the size of the difference matters more than the p.
-   Report **missing** counts, and the **number analysed**.
-   Export for a paper with `as_flex_table()` (Word) or `as_gt()` (HTML/PDF).

### What `add_p()` does by default

| Variable | 2 groups | 3 or more groups |
|---|---|---|
| Number | Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann–Whitney), **whatever the distribution** | Kruskal–Wallis |
| Category | chi-square **without** Yates' correction if **every** expected count is ≥ 5, otherwise **Fisher's exact** | same rule |

The default for categories is stricter than Cochran's rule (Fisher as soon as **any** expected count is below 5), which is
safe. The default for numbers never uses a t-test: you choose that yourself, below.

### Which tests gtsummary can run, and which it cannot

| gtsummary does it | How |
|---|---|
| Welch t-test, one-way ANOVA, **Welch ANOVA** | `add_p(test = x ~ "t.test")`, `"aov"`, `"oneway.test"` |
| Mann–Whitney, Kruskal–Wallis, Mood's median test | `"wilcox.test"`, `"kruskal.test"`, `"mood.test"` |
| Chi-square (with or without Yates), Fisher, test of two proportions | `"chisq.test"`, `"chisq.test.no.correct"`, `"fisher.test"`, `"prop.test"` |
| Monte Carlo p for chi-square or Fisher | `test.args = x ~ list(simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 10000)` |
| **Paired** t, Wilcoxon signed-rank, **McNemar** | long data, `"paired.t.test"`, `"paired.wilcox.test"`, `"mcnemar.test"` with `group = id` |
| **Difference with 95% CI**, Cohen's d, Hedges' g, standardised difference (SMD) | `add_difference()`, `test = x ~ "cohens_d"`, `"smd"` |
| Adjusted difference (ANCOVA), random-intercept model for clustered data | `add_difference(test = x ~ "ancova", adj.vars = ...)`; `"lme4"` with `group =` |
| Confidence interval of each mean or percentage | `add_ci()` |
| Multiple-testing adjustment | `add_q(method = "holm")` (or `"fdr"`) |
| Regression tables (linear, logistic, Cox, Poisson …) | `tbl_regression()`, `tbl_uvregression()` |
| Survey-weighted tests, log-rank | `tbl_svysummary()` + `add_p()`; `tbl_survfit()` + `add_p()` |
| **Any other test** | your own function in `add_p(test = x ~ my_test)` (example below) |

| Not in gtsummary (run it yourself, report it in the text or a separate table) | Use |
|---|---|
| Checking assumptions: Shapiro–Wilk, Q-Q plots, Levene | `shapiro.test()`, `ggplot() + stat_qq()`, `car::leveneTest()` |
| Repeated measures with **3 or more** time points (sphericity, Greenhouse–Geisser), Friedman | `rstatix::anova_test()`, `friedman.test()` |
| **Post hoc** tests after ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis | `TukeyHSD()`, `rstatix::games_howell_test()`, `rstatix::dunn_test()` |
| Correlation (Pearson, Spearman) | `cor.test()` |
| Effect sizes for tables and ranks: Cramér's V, rank-biserial r, η², Kendall's W | `effectsize::cramers_v()`, `rstatix::wilcox_effsize()`, `effectsize::eta_squared()` |
| One-sample tests against a benchmark | `t.test(x, mu = 100)`, `binom.test()` |
| Agreement: Bland–Altman, kappa, ICC | `BlandAltmanLeh`, `irr::kappa2()`, `irr::icc()` |

### A pipeline that chooses the test for each variable

The rule, the same as in the Statistical Analysis workshop (Session 2): a number is analysed **parametrically** (mean (SD),
t-test or Welch ANOVA) when it is roughly symmetric in **every** group (|skewness| < 1) and either the group has at least
30 people or, in a smaller group, Shapiro–Wilk does not reject normality; otherwise **rank-based** (median (IQR),
Mann–Whitney or Kruskal–Wallis). A category gets **chi-square** when at least 80% of expected counts are ≥ 5 and none is
below 1 (and, in a 2 × 2 table, none below 5); otherwise **Fisher**.

```{r}
library(readxl)
library(janitor)

skewness <- function(x) { x <- x[!is.na(x)]; mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3 }

# One row per variable: the evidence, the decision, the test and the summary to show
choose_tests <- function(data, by, continuous, categorical) {
  k <- n_distinct(data[[by]])
  cont <- map(continuous, \(v) {
    g <- map(split(data[[v]], data[[by]]), \(x) x[!is.na(x)])
    n <- lengths(g); sk <- map_dbl(g, skewness)
    sw <- map_dbl(g, \(x) if (length(x) < 30) shapiro.test(x)$p.value else NA)
    tibble(variable = v, smallest_n = min(n), largest_skew = max(abs(sk)),
           shapiro_small_groups = if (all(is.na(sw))) NA else min(sw, na.rm = TRUE),   # NA: no group under 30
           parametric = all(abs(sk) < 1 & (n >= 30 | sw > 0.05), na.rm = TRUE))
  }) |> list_rbind() |>
    mutate(test = case_when(parametric & k == 2 ~ "t.test", parametric ~ "oneway.test",
                            k == 2 ~ "wilcox.test", TRUE ~ "kruskal.test"),
           statistic = if_else(parametric, "{mean} ({sd})", "{median} ({p25}, {p75})"))
  cat <- map(categorical, \(v) {
    e <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(table(data[[v]], data[[by]]))$expected)
    tibble(variable = v, table = paste(dim(e), collapse = " x "),
           smallest_expected = min(e), pct_below_5 = 100 * mean(e < 5),
           test = if_else((all(dim(e) == 2) & min(e) < 5) | mean(e < 5) > 0.2 | min(e) < 1,
                          "fisher.test", "chisq.test.no.correct"))
  }) |> list_rbind()
  list(continuous = cont, categorical = cat)
}
```

Applied to the workshop's practice data (631 adults; only 27 with diabetes, so small expected counts appear):

```{r}
p <- read_excel(c("../data/prac_modded.xlsx", "data/prac_modded.xlsx")[file.exists(c("../data/prac_modded.xlsx", "data/prac_modded.xlsx"))][1]) |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(past_history_of_diabetes, c("no", "yes"), c("No diabetes", "Diabetes")),
         wealth   = factor(wealth_index_of_participants, c("poorest", "poorer", "middle", "richer", "richest")),
         weight   = if_else(weight < 20, weight * 10, weight))    # the one entry error (see the workshop, Session 1)

rules <- choose_tests(p, by = "diabetes",
                      continuous  = c("age_of_participants", "height", "weight", "glucose_level_mg_d_l"),
                      categorical = c("sex_of_participants", "past_history_of_hypertension", "wealth",
                                      "marital_status_of_participants"))
rules$continuous  |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 2))) |> knitr::kable()
rules$categorical |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 2))) |> knitr::kable()
```

The decisions go straight into the table, so the summary and the test always match:

```{r}
#| warning: false
# (warning: false hides chi-square's "approximation may be incorrect" note for wealth, which the rule accepted)
tests <- c(setNames(as.list(rules$continuous$test), rules$continuous$variable),
           setNames(as.list(rules$categorical$test), rules$categorical$variable))
stats <- c(setNames(as.list(rules$continuous$statistic), rules$continuous$variable),
           list(all_categorical() ~ "{n} ({p}%)"))

p |>
  select(diabetes, all_of(c(rules$continuous$variable, rules$categorical$variable))) |>
  tbl_summary(by = diabetes, statistic = stats, digits = all_continuous() ~ 1,
              label = list(age_of_participants ~ "Age (years)", height ~ "Height (cm)", weight ~ "Weight (kg)",
                           glucose_level_mg_d_l ~ "Random glucose (mg/dL)", sex_of_participants ~ "Sex",
                           past_history_of_hypertension ~ "Known hypertension", wealth ~ "Wealth index",
                           marital_status_of_participants ~ "Marital status")) |>
  add_p(test = tests, pvalue_fun = label_style_pvalue(digits = 3)) |>
  add_q(method = "holm") |>
  bold_labels()
```

-   With only 27 adults in the diabetes group, Shapiro–Wilk also decides for that group. **Age** fails (skewness 1.0, and
    Shapiro–Wilk p = 0.02 among the diabetics): Mann–Whitney, median (IQR). Height, weight and glucose pass: Welch t, mean (SD).
-   **Glucose** looks very skewed in the whole sample (skewness 3.6, workshop Session 2), but that is two groups mixed
    together: **within** each group it is roughly symmetric, and that is what the t-test needs. Welch copes with the very
    different SDs (14 vs 58 mg/dL).
-   Known hypertension (2 × 2, an expected count of 2.6) and marital status (a third of expected counts below 5) go to
    **Fisher**; wealth (exactly 20% below 5, none below 1) stays with chi-square.
-   The **footnotes** name the test used for each row, so the methods section can say: *"Numbers were compared with
    Welch's t-test when roughly symmetric (|skewness| < 1, and Shapiro–Wilk p > 0.05 in groups under 30) and with the
    Mann–Whitney U test otherwise; categories with the chi-square test, or Fisher's exact test when expected counts were
    small. p-values were adjusted with Holm's method."*
-   **`add_q()`** adds Holm-adjusted p-values: a Table 1 makes many comparisons at once.

For **three or more groups** the same function picks Welch ANOVA (`oneway.test`) or Kruskal–Wallis:

```{r}
choose_tests(p, by = "wealth", continuous = c("age_of_participants", "height", "weight"),
             categorical = c("sex_of_participants", "past_history_of_diabetes"))$continuous |>
  select(variable, largest_skew, parametric, test) |> knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## A rule chosen from the data must be fixed in advance
Choosing each test by looking at the data is common in Table 1 and acceptable when the **rule** is written in the
protocol or analysis plan and reported. Do not try both tests and keep the smaller p. For the **main** comparison of a
study, decide the test from the design and the known behaviour of the variable (length of hospital stay and
triglycerides are skewed in every study), not from this pipeline.
:::

### Paired data: before and after in the same people

Put the data in **long** form (one row per person per visit) and tell gtsummary who is who with `group =`:

```{r}
pain <- p |>
  select(s_no, pain_foot_bfr, pain_foot_aftr) |>
  pivot_longer(-s_no, names_to = "visit", values_to = "foot_pain") |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, c("pain_foot_bfr", "pain_foot_aftr"), c("Before", "After")))
fbs <- p |>
  select(s_no, fbs_presentation, fbs_6_months) |>
  pivot_longer(-s_no, names_to = "visit", values_to = "fbs") |>
  mutate(visit = factor(visit, c("fbs_presentation", "fbs_6_months"), c("Before", "After")))

tbl_merge(list(
  pain |> tbl_summary(by = visit, include = foot_pain, label = foot_pain ~ "Foot pain") |>
    add_p(test = foot_pain ~ "mcnemar.test", group = s_no),
  fbs |> tbl_summary(by = visit, include = fbs, statistic = fbs ~ "{mean} ({sd})", label = fbs ~ "Fasting glucose (mg/dL)") |>
    add_p(test = fbs ~ "paired.t.test", group = s_no)
), tab_spanner = c("**Foot-care programme**", "**Lifestyle programme**"))
```

Without `group =`, gtsummary would compare the two visits as if they were different people. With **three** visits, use
`rstatix::anova_test()` or `friedman.test()` (not in gtsummary).

### Differences with confidence intervals

A p-value alone does not say how big a difference is. `add_difference()` adds the difference and its 95% CI:

```{r}
p |>
  select(diabetes, age_of_participants, height, weight) |>
  tbl_summary(by = diabetes, statistic = all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
              label = list(age_of_participants ~ "Age (years)", height ~ "Height (cm)", weight ~ "Weight (kg)")) |>
  add_difference()                       # Welch t-test: difference in means (No diabetes - Diabetes)
```

Use `add_difference(test = everything() ~ "smd")` for **standardised** differences: the usual balance check for a
randomised trial or a matched study, where p-values for baseline differences are not meaningful.

### Your own test: chi-square test for trend

For an **ordered** category (education, wealth) against a yes/no outcome, a test for **trend** asks one sharper question
than the ordinary chi-square ("does the percentage rise or fall across the levels?"). gtsummary has no built-in trend test,
but `add_p()` accepts any function that returns a p-value and a method name:

```{r}
trend_test <- function(data, variable, by, ...) {
  tab <- table(data[[variable]], data[[by]])
  res <- prop.trend.test(tab[, "Yes"], rowSums(tab))       # Cochran–Armitage chi-square for trend
  tibble::tibble(p.value = res$p.value, method = "Chi-square test for trend")
}

ncd |>
  mutate(education = factor(education, c("No schooling", "Primary", "Secondary", "Graduate+"))) |>
  select(htn, education) |>
  tbl_summary(by = htn, percent = "row", label = education ~ "Education",
              missing_text = "Missing") |>
  add_p(test = education ~ trend_test) |>
  modify_spanning_header(all_stat_cols() ~ "**Hypertension**")
```

Hypertension falls steadily with education (44% with no schooling to 25% among graduates). The same pattern works for
any test R can run: the function receives the data, the variable and the grouping column.

### Checklist for a table with p-values

-   The **summary** matches the **test**: mean (SD) with t-test or ANOVA, median (IQR) with rank-based tests.
-   The **rule** for choosing tests is written in the methods; the footnotes name each test.
-   **Paired** or clustered data use `group =`; never compare visits as independent groups.
-   Report **missing** values (`missing_text`); tests use the people with data for that variable.
-   Many comparisons: **adjust** (`add_q()`) or call them descriptive.
-   Show **sizes**, not only p: `add_difference()` or `add_ci()`.
-   Randomised trial baseline: **no** p-values; standardised differences if needed.
-   What gtsummary cannot do (assumption checks, post hoc tests, 3+ repeated measures, correlation, agreement) goes in the
    text or a separate table, with its own effect size and CI.

:::
